1.pericope_label: Is there not an appointed time to man upon earth? are not his days also like the days of an hireling? As a servant earnestly desireth the shadow, and as an hireling looketh for the reward of his work: So am I made to possess months of vanity, and wearisome nights are appointed to me. When I lie down, I say, When shall I arise, and the night be gone? and I am full of tossings to and fro unto the dawning of the day. My flesh is clothed with worms and clods of dust; my skin is broken, and become loathsome. My days are swifter than a weaver’s shuttle, and are spent without hope.

schools.summary: Delitzsch presses the noun exactly, that it means not a field hand's labour but active military service and so toil generally, corrects Ewald and others for rendering the next line as though it spoke of a slave, and states the comparison Job was heading for, death as the labourer's rest, while noting that he does not quite reach it. Ellicott turns to the body and names the disease, elephantiasis, in which the skin grows hard and rugged before it cracks and ulcerates, and supplies a rendering of the nights that catches their restlessness, the night long and the sufferer filled with tossings to and fro until the morning twilight.

Gill alone keeps the received sense of an appointed time, a set term for coming into the world and going out of it, which he confines to earth since neither heaven nor hell has a limited time to offer. He takes the servant's longing of shade from the midday heat, the verb meaning to gape or pant after it, and he is the first to see that the figure turns against itself, since the terms do not answer: instead of the refreshing shadow Job has months of vanity, and instead of the labourer's sweet sleep, wearisome nights. On the body he rejects the reading that makes this the corruption of the grave and canvasses the vermicular or pedicular disease, and he notes that some versions make the last image a racer while the Greek wrongly gives swifter than speech.

Clarke gives the Hebrew and renders the opening as a question whether there is not a warfare to miserable man upon earth, keeps the military half running when the nights are described, a man harassed like a soldier and always on the watch, thinks night rather than shade is longed for and supports it from Virgil and his commentator, and takes the worms literally, insects having laid eggs in open sores, breaking off because the image is too horrid to pursue. On the following phrase he says outright that all the commentators have missed the sense, which he takes for crusts of dried matter flaking from decaying pustules, and on the last he notes that the word means the weaver rather than his shuttle, doubts whether such an instrument existed then, cites an account of Aleppo where fine cloth was woven with every thread passed by hand, and still concludes that something of the kind must have been in view or the figure loses its force. Wesley shortens the longing to sunset, has the worms bred from the sores and the dust that on which the sufferer lay, and asks whether it is a crime to wish God would bring him to that joyful period.

Henry slips the warfare gloss into a parenthesis and then explains what Job is doing, excusing what he cannot justify. He heads off the objection in advance, that the longing for death is no claim that the time appointed of God may be anticipated but only language in which present uneasiness expresses itself. He also makes something of the setting, a man on the earth meanly placed beside the inhabitants of higher regions yet shown mercy in the place itself, being on the earth and not under it, and time here short according to the narrow bounds of this earth, whereas heaven cannot be measured.

7.pericope_label: O remember that my life is wind: mine eye shall no more see good. The eye of him that hath seen me shall see me no more: thine eyes are upon me, and I am not. As the cloud is consumed and vanisheth away: so he that goeth down to the grave shall come up no more. He shall return no more to his house, neither shall his place know him any more.

schools.summary: Delitzsch translates the hardest line as a broken sentence, thine eyes look for me and I am no more. Ellicott gives the same sense with the Greek and Latin behind it, calls the cloud a fine simile and says why it is apt, since whether a summer cloud thins away on the face of the sky or comes down in rain nothing passes more completely, being an appearance only that comes to nothing. On the last verse he is careful: the words need not be forced into a denial that Job believed in a future life, because on any view they are accurately true of man as we know him here, for even if he lives again elsewhere it is not in this world, and this world is what Job speaks of.

Gill takes the figure for life as breath rather than storm, a man's life sitting in his nostrils and being a vapour or a bubble, while allowing the noisy and blusterous sense too. He enters a qualification the others omit, that the vanishing must be limited to human sight, since the dead are still seen by the eyes of the omniscient God, in heaven, in hell and in the grave. He notes that the Targum reads smoke instead of cloud and heads off an objection, that clouds said elsewhere to return after rain are not the same clouds, adding that the same figure serves for pardon; and he takes the house both literally and figuratively, the second being the earthly house of the body, whose tenant does not return until the resurrection rebuilds it.

Clarke reports an alternative rendering in which the loss dreaded is not life but the sight of former mercies and declines it, the common translation giving a very good sense; he offers two constructions of the seeking eye, either that God can look him into nothing or that the look is the sentence of a man already judged to death; he states the cloud comparison flatly, that as the cloud never returns neither do the dead return to the living; and he denies that annihilation is meant in the last verse, only that the man will never again inhabit earth, noting that the word rendered grave covers the state of the dead, any deep pit, and sometimes hell. Wesley makes the look more terrible still, one angry look sufficing since God can look a man into eternity, turns the cloud into an observation from life, a cloud that looked great enough to eclipse the sun suddenly dispersed being exactly the life of man, and draws the inference that it concerns us to secure a better place, since this one will own us no more.

Henry notices the change of address and explains it, that Job, seeing his friends will not interrupt but have stopped attending, turns from them to God, since if men will not hear us God will and if men cannot help us he can. He then enters the caveat that governs the speech, that we must not go to school to Job to learn how to speak to God, there being a great mixture of passion and corruption in what he says, yet that if God is not extreme to mark what his people say amiss neither should we be; on this reading what Job asks is that God will either ease him or end him. He keeps both halves of the wind figure, life seeming loud and proving empty, soon gone and past recall, and recalls that God had compassion on Israel by remembering they were but flesh.

11.pericope_label: Therefore I will not refrain my mouth; I will speak in the anguish of my spirit; I will complain in the bitterness of my soul. Am I a sea, or a whale, that thou settest a watch over me? When I say, My bed shall comfort me, my couch shall ease my complaint; Then thou scarest me with dreams, and terrifiest me through visions: So that my soul chooseth strangling, and death rather than my life. I loathe it; I would not live alway: let me alone; for my days are vanity.

schools.summary: Ellicott says the reasonable course is to explain the hard verse from Scripture if possible and finds the key in the prophet's picture of sand set as a bound for the sea, adding that a writer familiar with Egypt would know the Nile, still called the sea, as a thing watched and diked so its overflow should not ruin the land. He renders the line about death literally as choosing death rather than these my bones, notes that some take it as a death by these my members, and glosses that as a death inflicted by himself; he then gives three readings of the thing loathed and re-reads the closing clause against the received version, preferring I shall not live for ever, so the line arrives as a ray of comfort rather than a refusal. Delitzsch translates the hard verse plainly as sea or sea-monster with a watch set over him.

Gill sets out the reasoning behind the decision to speak, that the common lot is warfare enough, that extraordinary afflictions have been added, that no good is to be had in the present life, and that he is going where no temporal good can be expected and from which there is no returning. He takes the comparison with the sea morally, the restless sea standing for abandoned sinners and the raging sea for persecutors, and answers that Job was the reverse of both, gentle to the poor and their rescuer. On the dreams he offers three causes without choosing among them, the distemper breaking his sleep and disturbing the imagination, the melancholy his afflictions had brought on, or Satan, in whose hands he had been placed. He denies outright that suicide is in view, neither self-strangling as Ahithophel did nor strangling as a judicial execution but, following Broughton, a choking by some suffocating disease, since death in any form is the stopping of a man's breath; and he offers his own alternatives for the closing phrase.

Clarke reports the Targum, which asks whether Job is condemned as the Egyptians drowned in the Red Sea or as Pharaoh in his sins, offers his own paraphrases, whether the speaker is as dangerous as the sea that it must be fenced or an ungovernable beast to be kept behind bars, and concludes that the received English is less exceptionable than any rendering yet offered. On the dreams he has no hesitation, holding that Satan was certainly permitted to haunt the imagination, so that the sufferer needed sleep and was afraid to close his eyes for the images waiting there. He takes the death of verse fifteen as an oppression like the nightmare felt in those broken slumbers, and keeps the refusal in the last verse, that length of days offered on these terms would be a boon to be spurned. Wesley reads the decision to speak as intention rather than surrender, that Job will plead with God for pity before he dies and ease himself by pouring out his complaint instead of smothering it, and draws the application, that in affliction we are apt to complain as though more were laid on us than there is occasion for, whereas we are never in heaviness but when there is need.

17.pericope_label: What is man, that thou shouldest magnify him? and that thou shouldest set thine heart upon him? And that thou shouldest visit him every morning, and try him every moment? How long wilt thou not depart from me, nor let me alone till I swallow down my spittle? I have sinned; what shall I do unto thee, O thou preserver of men? why hast thou set me as a mark against thee, so that I am a burden to myself? And why dost thou not pardon my transgression, and take away mine iniquity? for now shall I sleep in the dust; and thou shalt seek me in the morning, but I shall not be.

schools.summary: Ellicott renders the confession as putting the case that I have sinned, agrees that the swallowing of the spittle is doubtless proverbial, keeps the burden on Job himself and offers two figures for the mark, a target on which God expends all his arrows or a stumbling-block he comes into collision against, and explains the urgency of the prayer from Job's premise that sin was the origin of all disaster, adding that our Lord did not discourage the belief when he joined the assurance of forgiveness to the healing of the paralytic. Delitzsch settles the same clause on grammatical grounds, marking it hypothetical, and reads the following line as a burden to Thee rather than a burden to myself.

Gill takes the question about man as wonder rather than complaint, marvelling that God should magnify a frail and fallen creature at all and reading the magnifying as election and espousal to his Son. On the morning visitation he lets both senses stand and observes that the argument comes out the same either way, whether God visits in mercy, as the dayspring from on high and in mercies renewed every morning, or in punishment, which for his own people is fatherly chastisement. He notes that some supply an if before the confession, refuses the supplement and keeps it an affirmation, though of ordinary daily sin rather than the notorious course his friends alleged; and he takes lift up literally in the prayer for pardon, tracing the lifting from the sinner to the Son and away by blood.

Clarke frames the question about man as two ideas and adds the paraphrase of Calmet, in which Job protests that he is not worthy that God should concern himself about him. He calls the swallowing of the spittle proverbial, still current among the Arabs in nearly the same language and equivalent to asking for the twinkling of an eye. He reports Kennicott's proposal that the words about sin are addressed to Eliphaz rather than to God, and argues from Bildad's reply, which answers a man justifying himself, that Job does not criminate himself here, since otherwise the controversy would have ended and the book with it. Wesley takes only the first sense of the question, that man is not worthy of God's favour and is below his anger, widens the trial beyond affliction to prosperity and blessing, and glosses the spittle as a breathing time.

Henry sets out both possibilities for the question about man without choosing, either a passionate reflection on divine justice, as though the great God disparaged himself by contending with a creature so far beneath him, or a pious admiration of condescending grace. He supplies the pictures for the morning visitation, the daily call on a particular friend and the physician's round, and reads the trying every moment as feeling the pulse and observing the looks. He takes the spittle as description rather than proverb, supposing Job's distemper lay much in his throat and almost choked him; he reads a plain and ingenuous confession where others read a supposition, making the point that God had called Job perfect while Job says of himself that he has sinned, so a man may be upright who is not sinless. He hears the divine title both as observer and as preserver, noting that observer aggravates the confession while preserver is the right thing to plead in repentance, and draws the doctrinal conclusion that where God removes the guilt of sin he breaks its power.
